paper.title: Tax Reforms and Intertemporal Shifting of Wage Income: Evidence from Danish Monthly Payroll Records
paper.code_data_availability: The article page carries a dataset deposit: Kreiner, Claus Thustrup, Søren Leth-Petersen, and Peer Ebbesen Skov. …

registers.name_in_paper: the eIncome register (monthly payroll register from the Danish tax authority, SKAT)
registers.role: treatment assignment and outcomes: monthly wages and salaries of all employees
variables_mentioned: personal registration number of the employee

registers.name_in_paper: administrative registers at Statistics Denmark (socioeconomic information)
registers.role: controls: gender, age, marital status, geographic location of residence

registers.name_in_paper: administrative registers at Statistics Denmark (information on liquidity)
registers.role: controls / heterogeneity: financial assets (money in bank accounts, value of shares and bonds) at the end of 2008 and annual disposable income in 2008

registers.name_in_paper: administrative registers at Statistics Denmark (firm background information)
registers.role: heterogeneity: industry sector and firm size (number of employees)
variables_mentioned: number of employees in the firm

registers.name_in_paper: telephone survey conducted by the survey company Capacent Epinion (January 2011)
registers.role: outcomes: awareness of the shifting opportunity and of its legality
variables_mentioned: Q1: when it is most beneficial to have extra income paid out
Q2: whether postponing the payout is legal

registers.name_in_paper: Danish tax schedule (website of the Danish Ministry of Taxation, www.skm.dk)
registers.role: treatment: marginal tax rates on labor income before and after the 2010 reform (Table 1)

linkages: Employees linked to firms via the firm identifier in the eIncome register, giving industry sector and firm size
eIncome records linked to individual background information (gender, age, marital status, residence) and to liquidity information via the personal registration number at Statistics Denmark
Telephone survey responses merged at the individual level to the eIncome register (878 respondents: 588 T-group, 290 C-group)

sample.universe: All individuals in Denmark who were employed at some point between January 2008 and December 2011, as recorded in the eIncome register
sample.unit_of_observation: individual-month (monthly wage record); the shifting indicator and the LPM in equation (4) are at the individual level for January 2010
selection_rules: Keep individuals employed throughout 2008, i.e. with a wage record for every month of 2008
Keep individuals with positive income in all years (positive wage income in 2009 and 2010)
Restrict the main analysis to private-sector employees (separate analyses are run for local government employees)
Treatment group (T-group): average monthly gross earnings above DKK 35,000 in 2008 (percentile 75 of the full-time wage distribution)
Control group (C-group): average monthly gross earnings in the range DKK 30,000-35,000 in 2008
Allocation to tax bracket is based on 2008 income, before the tax reform could have affected income
sample.period: January 2008 - December 2011; estimation of specification (5) on January 2009 - December 2010
sample.n_observations: 324,126 observations in the linear probability model of Table 3
sample.n_individuals: 328,679 individuals, of which 219,179 in the treatment group (text, Section I); the note to Figure 3 reports 219,598 in the T-group and 109,672 in the C-group, and the note to Table 5 reports 219,179 in the T-group and 109,500 in the C-group, out of a total of 329,270 taxpayers

construction_notes: Percentage wage changes are computed as w_{y,m,i} = (z_{y,m,i} - z_{2008,m,i}) / zbar_{2008,i}, i.e. relative to the individual's average monthly gross earnings in 2008; percentage changes rather than a log transformation are used because earnings may be zero or close to zero in some months, for example due to income shifting
2008 rather than 2009 is used as the baseline year because 2009 income is influenced by the shifting behavior; Table A2 shows results are similar with 2009 as baseline

Shifting indicator (formula (3)) equals one if income in a month is more than 50 percent above the 2008 average monthly level and income in the preceding month is more than 50 percent below it; 25/25 and 75/75 percent criteria give shares of shifters of 3.0 and 1.9 percent respectively
Liquidity is measured as the 2008 value of stocks, bonds and deposit accounts relative to average monthly net-of-tax wages (0-1, 1-2 and 2+ months)
The incentive calculation in Figure 1 assumes the taxpayer has the same monthly earnings level in all months and uses a 2 percent growth rate in nominal wages from 2009 to 2010
Marginal tax rate computed as LMC + (1 - LMC) x (RT + BT + MT + TT + CT); 62.8 percent above the DKK 377,000 cutoff in 2009 and 56.0 percent above the DKK 424,000 cutoff in 2010
Confidence intervals in Table 3 are based on bootstrapped standard errors with 1,000 replications; standard errors in specification (5) are clustered at the individual level

claims.statement: The 2010 Danish tax reform changed the reported monthly wage income of employees with a strong incentive to shift income (T-group) relative to the control group by -3 percent in November 2009.

treatment.label: The Danish 2010 tax reform: reduction of the top marginal tax rate on labor income from 62.8 percent in 2009 to 56.0 percent in 2010 (an 18 percent increase in the net-of-tax rate), i.e. belonging to the treatment group with a strong incentive to shift income

register_source.value: eIncome register (monthly payroll register of the Danish tax authority, SKAT); group assignment from average monthly wage income in 2008

definition.value: Treatment group (T-group) = private-sector employees with average monthly gross earnings above DKK 35,000 in 2008 (percentile 75), who face the abolished middle tax and the reduced top-bracket rate; control group (C-group) = employees with average monthly income DKK 30,000-35,000 in 2008, whose net-of-tax rate rises only 2 percent. Allocation to tax bracket is based on 2008 income, before the reform could have affected income.

timing.value: Reform proposed 1 March 2009, passed 28 May 2009, in force from 1 January 2010; treatment status assigned on 2008 income

outcome.label: Percentage change in monthly wage income of the T-group relative to the C-group (w in formula (2))

register_source.value: eIncome register (monthly payroll register from the Danish tax authority, SKAT)

definition.value: w_{y,m,i} = (z_{y,m,i} - z_{2008,m,i}) / zbar_{2008,i}: the difference between an individual's gross wage income in month m of year y and in the same month of 2008, as a percentage of that individual's average monthly gross earnings in 2008; then averaged over the T-group minus the average over the C-group (formula (2)).

timing.value: monthly, January 2008 - January 2011; baseline months are the months of 2008

units.value: percent of the individual's average monthly gross wage income in 2008 (T-group relative to C-group)

magnitude.interpretation: The wage income of the T-group is 3 percent below its counterfactual level in November 2009, the second-to-last month before the reform took effect.

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector employees with average monthly gross earnings above DKK 35,000 in 2008 (the treated group), relative to employees earning DKK 30,000-35,000
estimand.time_horizon: November 2009, i.e. 2 month(s) before the reform took effect on 1 January 2010

population.description: Danish private-sector employees who were employed in every month of 2008 and had positive wage income in 2009 and 2010; treatment group = average monthly gross earnings above DKK 35,000 in 2008 (percentile 75 of the full-time wage distribution), control group = average monthly gross earnings DKK 30,000-35,000 in 2008
subgroups_defined: top-five wage earners within the firm
liquid assets of 0-1, 1-2 and 2+ months of net-of-tax wages
population.selection: Individuals with irregular earnings and temporary employment contracts (including children) are implicitly excluded by requiring a wage record in every month of 2008; the self-employed are not analysed separately, though individuals who are both wage earners and self-employed are included.

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish 2010 tax reform, proposed 1 March 2009, passed 28 May 2009 and effective 1 January 2010, cut the marginal tax rate on labor income for high-wage earners from 62.8 to 56.0 percent, creating an incentive to postpone wage payments from 2009 into 2010; employees with negligible incentive form the control group.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common wage growth rate of the T-group and the C-group in the absence of the reform (common-trend / parallel-trends assumption underlying the difference-in-differences comparison).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the identifying assumption when formula (2) is introduced and again when the DiD ETI estimate is discussed; the paper concedes it may be problematic because young wage earners have steeper income profiles and dominate the control group, and it re-estimates with cohort, gender, marital status, region, industry and firm-size controls in Table A1.

key_assumptions.assumption: Assignment to the treatment and control group is predetermined: employees are allocated to a tax bracket on the basis of 2008 income, i.e. before the tax reform could have affected their income (no anticipation effect on the assignment variable).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated explicitly when the groups are defined; 2008 is before the reform was proposed (March 2009).

implies_edges.from: 2010 Danish tax reform / treatment-group status (strong incentive to shift wage income)
implies_edges.to: average monthly wage income in 2008 (variable assigning T-group vs C-group status)

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on being employed in every month of 2008 and having positive wage income in all years (full-time employees, private sector), so results are conditional on this selection.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the sample restriction; the paper notes that individuals with irregular earnings and temporary contracts are excluded.

implies_edges.from: employment in every month of 2008 and positive wage income in 2009 and 2010 (private sector)
implies_edges.to: sample inclusion: employed in every month of 2008 with positive wage income in all years, private sector

threats_discussed: Common-trend assumption may fail because young wage earners have steeper income profiles and are more dominant in the control group
Unobserved heterogeneity may imply that top income individuals experienced a different income development than the control group
Changes in bonus patterns and in exit rates from the labor market due to the financial crisis during 2009-2010
robustness_checks: Sample restricted to employees without any exit to unemployment during 2009 and 2010
Removing the self-employed completely from the sample
unresolved_confounders: Unobserved heterogeneity implying top-income individuals experienced a different income development from the control group; the paper concedes it cannot be ruled out and argues against it with the two-decade stability of Danish top income shares (Kleven and Schultz 2014).

estimator.value: Group means of individual percentage wage changes (formula (2)): average of w over the T-group minus the average over the C-group, computed month by month

estimation.specification: Monthly difference in average percentage wage change (relative to the same month of 2008, scaled by the individual's 2008 average monthly wage) between the T-group and the C-group; by construction the estimates are zero in the baseline months of 2008

sample_n.value: 219,598 employees in the T-group and 109,672 employees in the C-group (note to Figure 3)

ambiguities: The point estimates are stated in rounded prose ('3 percent and 5 percent below ... 9 percent above'); the printed 95 percent confidence interval for December 2009 is (-5.0, -4.2), whose midpoint is -4.6 rather than -5.

evidence.annotation: Panel B shows the difference between the wages in a given month and the same month in 2008 (as a percentage of the average monthly wage in 2008) for the T-group and measured relative to the C-group (in percentage points).

evidence.how: Horizon expressed in months relative to 1 January 2010, the date the reform took effect: November 2009 is -2 months.

value.lhs: w_{y,m} (average percentage wage change of the T-group relative to the C-group in month m of year y)
value.parameter_of_interest: w_{y,m}, the month-specific T-group minus C-group difference
value.normalisation: Each individual's monthly income change is divided by that individual's average monthly gross earnings in 2008 (formula (1)); by definition the estimates are zero in the baseline months of 2008.

value.claimed_domain: Countries where intertemporal shifting of wage income is legal; the authors note that shifting of wage and salary income across years for legal tax avoidance is not permitted in the United States, where such effects may therefore be less pronounced, though they argue the difference may not be large in practice.
boundary_conditions: Applies to wage and salary income only; stock options and other forms of compensation are not observed in the data

falsification.condition: The shifting interpretation would be refuted if systematic income effects appeared in other months, or in the middle-income control group with only negligible changes in incentives; the paper reports it detects none.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Sensitivity analysis restricting the sample to employees without any exit to unemployment during 2009 and 2010 (described as having no significant effect; estimates not reported)
Estimates removing the self-employed completely from the sample (described as having only negligible effects; estimates not reported)

regressors: w_{y,m} (T-group minus C-group difference, formula (2))
target_designation.reasoning: Formula (2) defines w_{y,m} as the T-group minus C-group difference in monthly wage growth, the object the figure estimates.

basis.reasoning: The November 2009 dip of -3 percent is one of the two pre-reform months named in the introduction's 'nearly 10 percent higher in January 2010 and correspondingly lower in November and December 2009'.

subgroups_defined: top-five wage earners within the firm

definition.value: (1 - tau_{y,i})/(1 - tau_{2009,i}), the individual's net-of-tax rate in year y relative to 2009. The reform cut the top marginal rate from 62.8 to 56.0 percent, an 18 percent increase in the net-of-tax rate for the T-group, against 2 percent for the C-group.

timing.value: 2009 versus 2010; treatment status assigned on 2008 income

outcome.label: Reported monthly wage income, measured as the percentage change relative to the individual's 2008 average monthly gross earnings (w in formula (1)), for income group P99 <= income

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated explicitly when the groups are defined; 2008 is before the reform was proposed (March 2009).
